lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3, what are the three Rs? (Reduce, reuse, recycle.) One person helps; a whole class helps more, and can prove it. Today: how to plan a class action for the planet and measure what changed.
Start with a question about your own place: How much rubbish do we throw away? How much energy do we waste? Which wild creatures live here? Choose one problem you can really change.
Scientists measure before they change anything. Weigh the class rubbish for a week, count lights left on, or count insects in one square metre of grass. This first measurement is called a baseline.
Set a clear goal, like 'Cut our rubbish by a quarter in a month.' Plan who does what: posters, a reuse box, a switch-off monitor, a wildflower patch. Small, steady actions by everyone work best.
Measure again in exactly the same way. The class rubbish fell from 40 kg to 30 kg a week: 40 − 30 = 10 kg less. 10 out of 40 is a quarter: 25% less. Goal reached!
Keep the test fair: the same days, the same scales, the same bins. If something else changed, like a holiday week, say so. Honest results, even disappointing ones, help the next plan.
Share what you found with a chart and a short report, and ask others to join in. A class action links to the world's 17 Global Goals: many small actions in many places add up to a big change.
Try it in the world: count the trees in one part of your world, and plant more for a week. Then count again, and build a bar chart of blocks to show the change. Next: what do we owe each other?

exercises.hint: Scientists measure before they change anything.
choices: a first measurement before any change
the line at the bottom of a page
a line on a sports field
exercises.explain: A baseline is the first measurement, taken before the action starts.

exercises.prompt: It helps to measure before and after an action.
exercises.hint: How else would you know what changed?
exercises.explain: True: measuring before and after shows what really changed.

exercises.hint: A clear goal says what, how much and by when.
choices: Cut our rubbish by a quarter in a month.
exercises.explain: 'Cut our rubbish by a quarter in a month' says what, how much and by when.
Reduce, reuse, recycle: use less, use things again, then make them into new things.

exercises.prompt: Only big actions by grown-ups can help the planet.
exercises.hint: What do many small actions add up to?
exercises.explain: False: many small actions by many people add up to a big change.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a class action in order.
exercises.hint: You need a 'before' to compare with.
exercises.explain: Choose, measure a baseline, act, then measure again and share.

exercises.prompt: The class threw away 36 kg of rubbish in week 1 and 27 kg in week 4. How many kg less was that?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller from the bigger.

exercises.prompt: Why measure in exactly the same way each time?
exercises.hint: What if you used different scales?
choices: so the results are fair to compare
exercises.explain: Measuring the same way keeps the test fair, so the results can be compared.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: reduces waste or does not help?
exercises.hint: Does it mean less rubbish in the bin?
exercises.explain: Reduces waste: a reuse box, both sides of paper, refillable bottles. Does not help: throwing food away, extra plastic.

exercises.prompt: Honest results are useful even when the goal is not reached.
exercises.hint: What can you learn from a plan that did not work?
exercises.explain: True: honest results help the next plan work better.

exercises.prompt: The rubbish fell from 50 kg to 40 kg a week. By what percentage did it fall?
exercises.hint: Find how many kg less, then how many that is for every 100 kg.
exercises.explain: 50 − 40 = 10 kg less. 10 out of 50 is 20 out of 100: 20%.

exercises.prompt: There was a holiday week with no school during the test. What should the class do?
exercises.hint: Would a week with no school be a fair week to compare?
choices: say so, because it changes the results
count it as a normal week
exercises.explain: Say so honestly: fewer people meant less rubbish, not the plan.

exercises.prompt: Why share results with a chart?
exercises.hint: Which is quicker to read: a chart or a long list?
choices: others can see the change quickly
exercises.explain: A chart shows the change at a glance, so others can see it and join in.

exercises.prompt: The class planted 12 wildflower patches. Each one attracts about 15 bees. About how many bees is that?
exercises.hint: Multiply the patches by the bees for each.

exercises.prompt: How does a class action link to the world's Global Goals?
exercises.hint: Think of many classes in many countries.
choices: many small actions add up to big change
the Goals are only for grown-ups
exercises.explain: Many small actions in many places add up to the big changes the Goals aim for.
